newsitem.title: USA: Black soldier discharged for painting swastikas.
newsitem.headline: Black soldier discharged for painting swastikas.

text.p: An black sergeant has been ordered discharged from a U.S. Army special forces unit for painting red swastikas on barracks doors at Fort Bragg last summer, base officials said on Thursday.

The vandalism took place in the early morning hours of July 16, when someone spray-painted two-foot-high swastikas on the doors to eight rooms inside the barracks. Six of the rooms were occupied by black soldiers.
The incident caught the attention of President Clinton, who said at the Democratic convention Green Berets "do not deserve to have swastikas painted on their doors."
Sgt. Robert L. Washington, has denied painting the symbols, used by the Nazi regime earlier this century.
Carol Jones, a spokeswoman for Fort Bragg, said Washington was also ordered discharged for failing a physical fitness test.

A support soldier for the Army elite forces commonly known as the Green Berets, Washington, 31, enlisted in the Army in 1990 after graduating from the University of Georgia with a degree in sociology.

Washington has said he was being set up and that some of the evidence the government presented was suspect, including paint chips on his shoes. Army laboratory tests showed the paint matched that on the doors, but was dry when it got on the shoes.
Washington could appeal to the Army Board for the Correction of Military Records, but it was not immediately known whether he would do so.

Maj.-Gen. Kenneth Bowra, the commanding officer at Fort Bragg, approved the discharge after a three-man administrative board recommended it. The incident was not handled through a court martial because the alleged misconduct was not a violation of the Code of Military Justice.
